one_liner: C++23 port of Rust simdxml: SIMD structural XML indexer with XPath 1.0, claiming 1.04-1.24x pugixml parse throughput.
what_it_does: Parses an XML buffer into a read-only structure-of-arrays index of tag offsets, types, depths, parents and text ranges. Names and text come back as string_views into your buffer, and you query the index through navigation calls or compiled XPath 1.0. It is not a pugixml drop-in. The entry point is rai::xml::parse(std::span<const std::byte>), which returns std::expected<XmlIndex, SimdXmlError>. Nodes are integer indices, the tree cannot be modified or serialized, and the caller must keep the input alive. Extras include a query-driven selective parse (parse_for_query), a multi-threaded chunked parse (parse_parallel), a .sxi on-disk index cache and C14N output.
how_it_is_fast: Stage 1 classifies each 64-byte chunk with PSHUFB nibble-table lookups (the simdjson technique). This yields u64 bitmasks for '<', '>', both quote types, '-', ']', '/', '?' and whitespace. AVX2, SSE4.2, NEON and scalar backends are all compiled in and picked at run time via [[gnu::target]]. Stage 2 is a scalar state machine that jumps between set bits with countr_zero instead of scanning bytes, and popcounts of the '<'/'>' masks size every output vector exactly once. The parse only records offsets. It does no per-node allocation, no entity decoding and no attribute splitting (attributes are re-scanned on demand). ensure_indices() later builds CSR child lists with an AVX2 prefix sum, plus pre/post-order numbers for O(1) ancestor checks.
when_to_use: Read-only extraction or XPath 1.0 queries over trusted, well-formed XML of about 1-10 MB. The README shows a 4-24% faster parse and 12-19% lower peak RSS than pugixml at this size.
Markup- and attribute-dense documents with comments, CDATA and PIs. These are skipped with bitmask tricks (e.g. dash & dash>>1 & gt>>2 finds '-->') rather than byte loops.
Shipping one x86-64 binary built with GCC/Clang to mixed fleets from SSE4.2-only to AVX2 CPUs, or to AArch64 NEON, with no -mavx2 build flags.
Repeated queries over the same large files. load_or_parse() can reuse a persisted .sxi index, and parse_for_query() indexes only the tags a query names plus their ancestors.
C++23 codebases that want std::expected error handling and zero-copy string_view results.
when_not_to_use: Untrusted or possibly malformed input. It does not check well-formedness: mismatched close tags such as are accepted, and the MismatchedCloseTag error is never raised. DOCTYPE is skipped only up to its first '>', and .sxi files are documented as trusted caches only.
Documents nested deeper than 32 levels, which get degraded parent links. Also documents that rely on DTD-defined entities: only the five predefined entities and numeric references are decoded.
Any need to modify or write XML. Unlike pugixml, there is no mutable DOM and no serializer.
MSVC builds. has_avx2()/has_sse42() return false under _MSC_VER, so parse falls back to the plain memchr scanner and the SIMD path that was benchmarked is never used.

Production code that needs maturity. The repo has 0 stars, was created 2026-09-07 and is at v0.1.0. It has no tests, CI or benchmark code, and it does not include the Rust crate's XPath conformance suites.

integration.min_toolchain: C++23 (uses std::expected, std::format, std::jthread) and CMake 3.20+; exact compiler versions not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 with runtime AVX2/SSE4.2/scalar dispatch under GCC/Clang (scalar only under MSVC); aarch64 with NEON (used when PMULL/crypto is present, scalar otherwise); other architectures use the scalar fallback
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. ensure_indices() and build_name_index() mutate the index in place, so build them before sharing an XmlIndex across threads; CompiledXPath::eval takes a const XmlIndex&. build_indices() spawns two std::jthreads above 10K tags, and parse_parallel() spawns one per chunk.

gotchas: Call ensure_indices() before running XPath. Without the CSR indices, each child-axis step does a linear scan over all tags, which goes quadratic on large documents. An earlier A/B in the README shows the lead over pugixml falling from 1.26-1.36x (parse only) to 1.02-1.10x once the full index is built.

Text and attribute values come back raw. Entities are decoded only when XPath extracts text, via XmlIndex::decode_entities, which allocates a std::string. Name IDs are u16 and clamp at 65,535 distinct tag names.

Some declared API is missing or stubbed. parse_for_xpath() and the string_view overload of load_or_parse() in simdxml.hpp have no definition, so calling them is a link error. Every batch function (eval_batch_text, count_batch, eval_batch_parallel, ...) returns an error in the shipped build because SIMDXML_HAVE_XPATH is never defined. Use parse_for_query() and the std::filesystem::path overload of load_or_parse() instead.

load_or_parse() writes a .sxi file next to the XML as a side effect. It hashes with FNV-1a, so it cannot read .sxi files written by the Rust crate (which uses xxh3). Accessors such as tag_type()/depth() use vector::at() and throw on out-of-range indices.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Parshred also has runtime-dispatched SIMD and XPath 1.0, and claims a much larger lead over pugixml (1.6-3.3x on its own benchmark). RapidXml has a third-party-measured lead over libxml2. Pick libsimdxml over them only if you want its lower-memory flat index with the .sxi cache and selective query parse, or need a scalar fallback on x86 CPUs without SSE4.2 (Parshred's README requires SSE4.2).
verified_claims_summary: In the README's base-clock run (i7-4850HQ fixed at 2.3 GHz with turbo off, fresh process per run, median of 9), parsing into the index ran at 245.7/261.4/285.2 MB/s versus pugixml 1.16 in-situ at 206.3/227.8/229.2 MB/s, a 1.15-1.24x lead on the project's own synthetic 1/5/10 MB XML. A later turbo-on run on the same laptop narrowed this to 283.0 vs 271.1 MB/s at 1 MB and 296.5 vs 278.5 MB/s at 10 MB (~1.04-1.06x). That run showed ~8% more CPU time than pugixml at 10 MB but 0.81-0.88x of pugixml's peak RSS. No compiler, flags or harness are published, and the libxml2 DOM figures (28.5-38 MB/s) are not a like-for-like comparison.
status_note: Actively developed by one author: 18 commits from 2026-09-07 to 2026-09-23, v0.1.0, no issues, releases or tags. It is MIT-licensed, keeps the Rust original's notice, and is a small dependency-free static library you could vendor, but it ships without tests.
